source_text:
Fragmentum in epistulam ad Philemonem (in catenis)
Phm
1,1 Ἐν πολλαῖς ἐπιστολαῖς ξένον τίθησι ῥῆμα τοῦ μέλλοντος εἰσάγεσθαι λόγου
κατασκευαστικόν, καὶ νῦν ἐπειδὴ ἔμελλεν ἀξιοῦν ὑπὲρ Ὀνησίμου τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ἀξίᾳ–
ἀξία δὲ αὐτοῦ τὸ δεδέσθαι–, τὸ ἀξιόπιστον τῆς παρακλήσεως δείκνυσιν.
thought_title: Paul's imprisonment as the credibility of his appeal
orientation: Oecumenius is explaining the opening of Paul's letter to Philemon, where Paul's mention of his own imprisonment prepares for his request on behalf of Onesimus.
pass_a_gloss: In many letters he places an unusual word that prepares for the argument about to be introduced, and now, since he was about to make an appeal on behalf of Onesimus by his own worth—and his worth is his imprisonment—, he shows the credibility of the appeal.

choices.why: Keeps the literal sense of ξένος as foreign or unusual, matching the source's claim that Paul places an unexpected term.
Renders the adjective's function of building toward or setting up the coming argument, without adding a noun.
Captures the sense of asking as worthy or fitting, in line with the glossary's appeal context.
Uses the glossary term 'worth' and keeps the instrumental dative force of the means by which Paul shows credibility.
Uses the glossary terms 'credibility' and 'appeal' and preserves the article-noun-genitive structure.

bible_refs.note: The fragment comments on this verse, where Paul mentions his imprisonment.

pass_b_english: In many letters Paul places a strange word that prepares for the argument he is about to introduce. Here too, since he was about to make a request on behalf of Onesimus, he shows the credibility of the appeal by his own worth—and his worth is the imprisonment.

problems.why: Same Greek concept rendered two ways; reader may think different technical terms.
Same act described as both 'appeal' and 'request' without distinction.
problems.fix: Use one term consistently, or note equivalence.

problems.why: Three variants for same concept; 'the imprisonment' is abstract where 'chains' is concrete.
Same Greek concept rendered 'unusual' in intro but 'strange' in all commentary sections.

fixed: Changed 'strange word' to 'unusual word' for consistency.
Changed 'the imprisonment' to 'his imprisonment' to make the reference to Paul's imprisonment clearer.
Changed 'a strange word' to 'an unusual word' for consistency.
